title: The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor
where_in_paper: Overview of the NetBurst Microarchitecture / In-Order Front End
decision: Adopted an Execution Trace Cache that stores already-decoded uops (up to 12K uops, hit rate similar to an 8-16KB conventional I-cache) and delivers up to 3 uops/cycle to the out-of-order core, instead of a conventional byte-oriented L1 I-cache.
alternatives_or_rejected: Rejected keeping the complicated IA-32 instruction decode logic in the main execution loop (the traditional approach). The paper states the trace cache 'removes the cumbersome decode logic from the main execution loop' and avoids the conventional I-cache's branch-target delay (delays getting through the branch predictor and then accessing the new location in the instruction cache).
rationale: Storing uops instead of bytes removes decode from the critical path; the trace cache also assembles uops into program-ordered traces from the predicted path, avoiding both the branch-predictor delay and the conventional I-cache access delay on taken branches. This was key to feeding the out-of-order core at high frequency.
outcome: The Pentium 4's front end can deliver up to 3 uops/cycle; most instructions execute from the trace cache, and the IA-32 decoder is invoked only on a trace cache miss. The paper notes this saves 3 pipeline stages and reduces power.

title: The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor
decision: Pursued significantly higher clock frequencies as a primary design goal, using deeply pipelined (hyper-pipelined) design — doubling pipeline depth to 20 stages vs. prior generation.
alternatives_or_rejected: Implicitly traded off IPC and branch-mispredict penalty: the paper and accompanying editorial note that deeper pipelines enable higher clock frequencies but come with the known cost of lower IPC, larger buffers, and higher mispredict latency. The design chose frequency leadership over IPC-per-cycle optimality.
rationale: The paper states the NetBurst microarchitecture 'features significantly higher clock rates and world-class performance.' The accompanying journal preface explicitly frames this as 'hyper-pipelined technology that doubles the pipeline depth to 20 stages, which significantly increases processor performance and frequency capability.' Frequency was treated as the primary lever for end-user-perceivable performance across media-rich applications.
outcome: Pentium 4 launched at 1.5 GHz (Nov 2000) on 0.18um CMOS, with a stated design target/roadmap to scale to 3 GHz and beyond; the journal preface notes the architecture was designed to scale to higher frequencies over subsequent process generations.

title: The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor
where_in_paper: Integer and Floating-Point Execution Units / Rapid Execution Engine
decision: Implemented a double-pumped (2x core clock) ALU — the Rapid Execution Engine — so that simple integer ALU ops execute at twice the core frequency (targeting 3 GHz ALU operation).
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper does not detail alternative execution-unit clocking schemes it considered, but the chosen design explicitly differs from running the ALU at core frequency. The accompanying journal preface highlights the Rapid Execution Engine as pushing 'the processor's arithmetic logic units to twice the core frequency, giving higher execution throughput.'
rationale: The paper states this is an 'extremely low latency double-pumped Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) that runs at 3GHz.' Running the ALU at 2x core frequency increases execution throughput for the simple integer operations that dominate integer workloads, without having to drive the entire core at that frequency.
outcome: The double-pumped ALU enables 3 GHz integer execution in a 1.5 GHz-core part; the paper reports it as a central element of the NetBurst execution engine, contributing to world-class performance in the targeted application areas.

title: The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor
decision: Designed a very low-latency Level 1 data cache accessed in just 2 clock cycles (4-way 8KB at 0.18um Willamette; later 16KB in Prescott), with aggressive speculation (speculative issue of load-dependent uops and selective replay).
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper does not explicitly enumerate alternative L1 latency targets, but the chosen design is framed against conventional L1 data caches with longer load-to-use latency. The design accepts the complexity of speculative issue and a replay mechanism to achieve the 2-cycle load-use latency.
rationale: The paper explicitly calls out 'the very low latency Level 1 data cache that is accessed in just two clock cycles' as a key feature. The accompanying slide material notes the distance between load scheduler and execution is longer than load latency, necessitating speculative issue of load-dependent uops and selective replay — a deliberate trade to keep the load-to-use latency at 2 cycles.
outcome: 2-cycle load-use latency for integer instructions (6 cycles for FP loads). The paper reports this contributes to the Pentium 4's performance in key application areas, particularly those with frequent memory accesses.

title: The Microarchitecture of the Pentium 4 Processor
decision: Added 144 new 128-bit SIMD instructions (SSE2) and tuned the microarchitecture for media-rich, content-creation, 3D, and multi-tasking workloads, as the explicit performance targets.
alternatives_or_rejected: The paper does not describe alternative ISA-extension sets considered. The design clearly chose to extend the SIMD instruction set substantially (144 new 128-bit SSE2 instructions) rather than relying solely on the existing SSE/MMX or on general-purpose integer/floating-point improvements.
rationale: The paper states the Pentium 4 is 'designed to deliver performance across applications where end users can truly appreciate and experience its performance' — specifically listing Internet audio/video, image processing, video content creation, speech recognition, 3D applications/games, multimedia, and multi-tasking. SSE2 'improves performance for multi-media, content creation, scientific, and engineering applications.' The 3.2 GB/s system bus is likewise justified by the need to 'provide the high data bandwidths needed to supply data to today's and tomorrow's demanding applications.'
outcome: The Pentium 4 delivers substantial gains over Pentium III in targeted applications (the paper shows SPEC2000, Winstone, video encoding, 3D gaming, video editing, MP3 encoding performance comparisons). It ships with 42M transistors, 217mm² die, 0.18um CMOS, 55W at 1.5GHz.
